# Results

## The article is already a strong noun lever

With the intervention off, inserting `an` versus `a` moves the
full-vocabulary noun distribution by TV \(0.937\) \([0.891,0.975]\) on
the 20 held-out prompts. A transformers-only baseline, with no sparse
intervention, gives TV \(0.940\) \([0.893,0.976]\) on the same 20 prompts
and TV \(0.975\) \([0.964,0.983]\) on 95 released `an`-target occupations;
the top-1 noun changes on every prompt in both splits. Any sparse handle
that flips the article therefore has a large, generic continuation
channel available before leftover internal control is considered.

## Free generation looks coordinated; replay and rescue split it

Amplifying S1 at \(5\times\) moves every held-out prompt to `an` and
changes the greedy noun on 19/20 prompts (@tbl-packaging). Concrete twins
include `a pilot`\(\rightarrow\)`an aviator` and
`a lawyer`\(\rightarrow\)`an attorney`. Matched random features and S3 do
not produce this switch. Those free-generation rates show that S1 is a
specific handle on orthographically article-class-consistent completions. They do not identify
the transmission route.

| Condition | \(N\) | \(\Delta\) art.\ logit favors `an` | Noun token preserved | Class shift | Wrapper-like | Package-like | Twin match |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| S1 \(5\times\) | 20 | 1.00 | 0.05 | 0.95 | 0.00 | 0.95 | 0.35 |
| S1 control | 20 | 0.70 | 1.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 |
| S3 \(5\times\) | 20 | 0.70 | 0.95 | 0.05 | 0.00 | 0.05 | 0.00 |

: Free-generation metrics (held-out occupations). Wrapper-like = generated
article moves and noun token stays; package-like = article-class-consistent
switch. These rates do not identify leftover noun control.
{#tbl-packaging}

The six-cell split does. S1 at \(5\times\) selects `an` on 20/20 prompts.
Inserting that treated article with the intervention **off** reproduces
the S1-on top-1 noun on 20/20 prompts. Across all 20 prompts, total TV is
\(0.893\), token-substitution TV is \(0.891\), and matched-prefix leftover
TV is \(0.028\) \([0.021,0.035]\) (@tbl-mediation; @fig-mediation A).
Cosine of \(E_M\) with \(E_T\) is \(0.949\) \([0.849,1.000]\); cosine of
\(E_R\) with \(E_T\) is \(0.124\) \([-0.112,0.355]\). Reconstruction
\(\|E_T-(E_M+E_R)\|_1\) is numerically zero (implementation check).
Frozen attention in the original S1 factorial yields the same qualitative
split.

| Attention | Total TV | Token-substitution TV | Leftover TV under treated article | Treated-token top-1 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Recomputed (primary) | 0.893 | 0.891 | 0.028 [0.021, 0.035] | 1.00 |
| Frozen (ablation) | 0.893 | 0.891 | 0.026 [0.020, 0.033] | 1.00 |

: S1 \(5\times\) six-cell split on all 20 held-out prompts. Intervals are
prompt-bootstrap 95\% intervals.
{#tbl-mediation}

The remaining forced cell supplies the complementary rescue. Restoring the
baseline article while leaving S1 active restores the baseline top noun on
20/20 prompts; the on/off distributional difference under that restored
article is TV \(0.030\) \([0.025,0.036]\) (@fig-mediation B). Thus the
treated article is sufficient to phenocopy the treated top noun, and the
baseline article is sufficient to rescue the baseline top noun despite the
upstream intervention. The leftover is not exactly zero: on seven listed
twins, target-minus-source \(\Delta\Delta\) is \(0.018\)
\([-0.071,0.107]\) under inserted `a` and \(0.089\) \([0.027,0.152]\)
under inserted `an`.

![S1 vector split, treated-token phenocopy and baseline-token rescue, and the prompt-aligned article-boundary jump under greedy decoding.](manuscript/figures/fig_mediation_decomposition.png){#fig-mediation width=92%}

## Prompt-aligned boundaries expose discrete causal amplification

We binary-search each prompt's S1 gain until its article margin is
bracketed by two gains separated by at most \(0.0039\), the chosen search
tolerance rather than an estimated physical width. Nineteen of 20 prompts
cross between gains 1 and 5. Under greedy decoding, the cross-boundary
noun change is TV \(0.938\) \([0.889,0.978]\); token substitution alone is
TV \(0.939\) \([0.889,0.977]\), with cosine \(0.9998\) \([0.9996,0.9999]\)
to the total (@fig-mediation C). Over the same interval, the fixed-`a`
distribution moves TV \(0.014\) \([0.009,0.019]\) and the fixed-`an`
distribution moves TV \(0.014\) \([0.010,0.017]\). The existence of an
argmax discontinuity is architectural and therefore unsurprising; the
empirical result is that this particular boundary exposes an approximately
\(0.94\)-TV continuation change while the two fixed-prefix paths remain
locally smooth. Greedy decoding therefore converts a tiny continuous
change into a nearly maximal downstream jump: a discrete causal
amplification, not a comparably large persistent latent rewrite.

The equal-looking endpoint margins in the original table require a
correction. Model, CLT, residual, and native logits are bfloat16; the
native dense grids contain only three distinct article margins. With the
same upstream states but a float32 normalization/unembedding readout, the
three audited grids contain 43 distinct margins across 51 gains and all
three cross zero. A float32 binary search narrows the bracket to
\(0.000244\); cross-boundary free TV remains \(0.992\)
\([0.989,0.997]\), whereas fixed-`a` and fixed-`an` TV are \(0.009\) and
\(0.004\), respectively. Thus \(0/0.125\) was a finite-precision artifact,
not evidence for a physical logit quantum; the high-gain argmax relay is
the robust result.

Nor is relay dominance confined to greedy decoding. Across article
temperatures \(0.1,0.25,0.5,1\), total TV declines smoothly from \(0.456\)
to \(0.057\), and the component produced by changing only the article
policy declines from \(0.454\) to \(0.055\). The matched-policy leftover
stays near \(0.015\); policy/total vector cosine ranges from \(0.999\) to
\(0.957\). At \(\tau=1\), `a`/`an` retain about 90% of article probability
mass. The public route is therefore a temperature-dependent gain channel,
not merely an argmax pathology (@fig-boundary-policy).

![Finite-precision audit and stochastic article-policy decomposition. Float32 final-head readout resolves the native bfloat16 plateaus; policy-mediated TV tracks total TV across temperature while the matched-policy leftover remains small.](manuscript/figures/fig_boundary_precision_policy.png){#fig-boundary-policy width=92%}

## Supporting controls: dose, families, and exploratory S2 localization

At \(1.5\times\), S1 writes `an` on only \(2/20\) prompts and total TV
collapses to \(0.065\). The leftover under inserted `an` is already
present: TV \(0.015\) and twin \(\Delta\Delta\) \(0.098\)
\([0.027,0.161]\). At \(3\times\), free `an` rises to \(0.90\), total TV
to \(0.802\), and token substitution still dominates. The dramatic
free-generation rewrite is therefore gated by whether the gain is large
enough to engage the article boundary of TV \(0.937\). The small leftover
under `an` is not created only by \(5\times\).

Appendix H compares \(5\times\) handles. Only S1 produces a large
free-generation article+noun switch, and that switch remains
token-substitution dominated. S3 does not move nouns. S2 never writes
`an`; greedy strings often derail, but under fixed `an` all seven twins
move toward their target (\(\Delta\Delta=+0.830\)). We classify S2 as
**exploratory evidence for a sparse fixed-token, vowel-class-aligned
effect mixed with free-generation disruption**. The S1 leftover under
`an` overlaps the random control, so we do not claim a specific noun plan
from that residual. An exploratory within-set decomposition identifies
L5/F383 as the principal carrier on the same 20 evaluation prompts
(Appendix I); it may encode vowel class, and only four matched controls
exist (\(p=0.20\)).

Appendices E--G establish cross-token reachability, stack sensitivity, and
estimand polarity: S1 changes later CLT activations; a layer-12 full-residual
reference moves target logits; and known article-only versus persistent
generators yield leftover TV \(0\) versus \(0.667\), respectively.

## Target-specific influence survives from the pre-article position

The stronger pre-article reference tests the missing
\(t\rightarrow t+2\) route. Layer 12 is selected on four development
pairs (Appendix J). On 12 disjoint same-article-class pairs, patching the
target-cued full residual at \(P\) while inserting the shared native
article `a` shifts the target-minus-source contrast by \(+1.339\) logits
\([1.021,1.677]\), compared with \(+0.215\) \([0.081,0.357]\) for ten
matched-norm random directions averaged within pair. The paired difference
is \(D=1.123\) \([0.858,1.440]\) (@fig-public-private A). The mean
full-vocabulary TV is \(0.073\) \([0.054,0.095]\). Before the patch the
mean target-minus-source gap is \(-4.302\) logits
\([-5.214,-3.422]\); the patch closes \(0.312\) \([0.265,0.371]\) of that
gap and moves mean target rank from \(12.2\) to \(4.4\), with top-10 entry
rising from \(8/12\) to \(11/12\). The target does not become top-1 on any
held-out pair, so this is target-specific private-state capacity, not
persistence-dominant behavioral control.

The same patch remains target-aligned under inserted `an`:
\(\Delta\Delta=+0.703\) \([0.526,0.875]\), versus \(+0.120\)
\([0.029,0.215]\) for matched random directions; the paired difference is
\(D=0.583\) \([0.417,0.761]\). Crossing public article with private patch
yields a public effect of \(+0.609\) logits \([0.224,0.984]\) with the
private patch off and \(-0.026\) \([-0.385,0.359]\) with it on
(@fig-public-private B). The interaction is
\(\Gamma=-0.635\) \([-0.839,-0.448]\). Matched random patches have a small
positive interaction \(+0.095\) \([0.019,0.171]\); the paired
target-minus-random interaction is \(-0.731\) \([-0.971,-0.498]\)
(@fig-public-private C). Article-prefix compatibility therefore modulates
the private target-state effect. Inserted `an` is mismatched for both
consonant-initial alternatives, so the negative interaction may reflect
grammatical mismatch, saturation, or support shifts toward other
vowel-initial nouns; we do not interpret it as an allocation trade-off
between two registers. Public token identity and private upstream state
are separately intervenable and non-additive in this target-constructed
reference. This does not show that a sparse feature allocates the same
lexical state between those routes.

![A pre-article target residual moves held-out nouns under a fixed visible article more than matched random directions; the raw \(2\times 2\) surface and the random-controlled interaction show that article-prefix compatibility modulates the private effect. Error bars are pair-bootstrap 95\% intervals.](manuscript/figures/fig_pre_article_public_private.png){#fig-public-private width=90%}

## Natural residuals isolate private influence but not a carrier switch

Natural occupation descriptions reproduce target-specific private
influence without naming the target noun. The pooled development sweep
selects layer 12. Under a fixed article, target patches move the
target-minus-source logit by \(0.776\) \([0.484,1.115]\) on 12
cross-class pairs and \(0.964\) \([0.667,1.266]\) on 12 same-class pairs.
Wrong-target patches yield only \(0.146\) and \(0.130\), respectively;
sign-reversed patches move the contrast in the opposite direction. The
effect decomposes into target-logit enhancement (\(+0.526\) cross-class;
\(+0.839\) same-class) plus smaller source suppression
(\(-0.250\) and \(-0.125\)). Target probability rises in both regimes,
while total occupation-vocabulary mass does not reliably increase.

Crucially, the natural patch changes the article on 0/12 pairs in either
regime. Consequently token-substitution TV is zero and all observed
free-path TV---\(0.049\) cross-class and \(0.059\) same-class---survives token
fixing. This strengthens the evidence for a natural private route, but it
does **not** reveal prompting regimes that reallocate causal state between
public and private carriers. Same versus cross article class changes
effect size, not channel identity (@fig-natural-regimes).

![Natural target-residual patches produce target-specific fixed-token effects in both article-class regimes, outperform wrong-target and matched-norm controls, but never change the article.](manuscript/figures/fig_natural_carrier_regimes.png){#fig-natural-regimes width=91%}

## Attribution predicts local efficacy, not transmission channel

Across 32 features selected on disjoint occupations, article attribution
predicts the induced article-margin change (Spearman \(\rho=0.530\),
two-sided permutation \(p=0.0021\)). It does not predict total TV
(\(\rho=-0.105\)), token-substitution TV (\(-0.176\)), treated-token
leftover TV (\(-0.052\)), or mean fixed-token TV (\(0.026\)); future-noun
attribution likewise predicts none of these interventional outcomes
(all \(|\rho|\le0.178\), all \(p\ge0.323\)). Attribution is calibrated for
the local contrast it scores, but does not by itself classify whether a
later effect will use the public or private route (@fig-attribution-calibration).

![Held-out calibration of attribution scores against causal outcomes. Article attribution predicts local article-margin movement but not downstream public or private channel strength.](manuscript/figures/fig_attribution_channel_calibration.png){#fig-attribution-calibration width=88%}
